script.opening: "Doctor, please — my skin is ruining my life. I've tried everything from the chemist and it's just got worse, and now it's scarring. I just want the strong tablets, Roaccutane, the ones that actually cure it. I can't keep living like this. Can you just refer me for it or prescribe it? I'll do anything to make it stop."

facts.text: Since 15, much worse in the last year. Face, chest and back. Lots of red, painful spots and some deep lumps on your jaw and back. Leaving pitted scars on your cheeks. On video you can show your face: many inflamed spots, several nodules on the jaw, and small pitted scars.
Benzoyl peroxide washes, salicylic acid, tea tree. The GP gave you a gel (adapalene) a year ago — used it for two months, it stung and did not help much. Never had antibiotic tablets.

You have stopped going to lectures in person, you keep your camera off on online seminars, you avoid mirrors and photos, you have stopped going out with friends and the gym. You turned down a part-time job because it was customer-facing.

facts.topic: Mood — only if asked directly and kindly
facts.text: Low most days for about three months. Sleeping a lot. If asked about suicidal thoughts: "Sometimes I think there's no point to anything. I've thought it'd be easier not to be here." No plan, no actions, no self-harm. You would not act on it "because of my mum". Nobody knows.
No other illnesses. No regular medicines. No allergies. No previous mental health problems. Not on any medicines that affect mood.
19, second-year engineering student, lives in a shared house. Drinks occasionally, no drugs, non-smoker. Close to your mum, who lives an hour away.
Roaccutane "cures it" — you have also read it can affect mood, "but I don't care, I'm already miserable".

Desperate and pleading, focused on getting the tablets. If the doctor dismisses it ("it's just spots", "you'll grow out of it"), go quiet and withdraw. If they take your skin seriously and ask how it is affecting you, open up slowly. Disclose the suicidal thoughts only if asked directly. Respond well to a plan that treats the skin now, refers to a dermatologist, and gets support for your mood.

ice.ideas: "Roaccutane is the only thing that will cure it."
ice.concerns: "It's scarring and it's ruining my life." Underneath (only if asked): how low you have got.
ice.expectations: "Refer me or prescribe it." You will accept a step-up plan and referral if you feel taken seriously.

cues: "I can't keep living like this." — say in the opening.
"I don't really go out any more." — say if asked about the impact.
"Sometimes I think there's no point." — say only if asked about your mood directly.

checkpoints.text: Takes the acne seriously (moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne with SCARRING failing topicals) and steps UP treatment appropriately — combination topicals, oral antibiotics WITH a topical (not antibiotic monotherapy) — and refers to DERMATOLOGY for ISOTRETINOIN given severity/scarring/psychological impact, recognising isotretinoin is specialist-prescribed (not GP-prescribed)

Explicitly ASSESSES MENTAL HEALTH and SUICIDE RISK: explores the profound psychological impact and asks directly about low mood and suicidal thoughts/plans/intent — recognising this is central, not incidental, and a safety issue

Explains isotretinoin REALITIES accurately: highly effective but dermatologist-prescribed with monitoring (lipids/LFTs), teratogenicity/Pregnancy Prevention Programme, mucocutaneous effects, and the MOOD/mental-health monitoring (MHRA) — so the mental-health assessment is part of safe isotretinoin care

Treats early to LIMIT SCARRING and validates that acne and its impact are NOT trivial — avoiding dismissive "it’s just spots" — while not simply processing a prescription request without addressing the distress
Makes a mental-health management plan: support for low mood (and risk management/crisis routes if suicidal ideation), and coordinates this with the acne/dermatology plan
Reaches the suicidal ideation behind "ruining my life", validates the genuine distress (without minimising the acne), and responds with compassion and a safety plan
Engages him as more than a prescription request — treating the whole young person — and explains why the mental-health side matters for him and for safe treatment

Safety-nets and follows up: the acne step-up and dermatology/isotretinoin referral, the mental-health support and crisis routes (urgent/111/crisis/A&E if risk), early follow-up, and coordination — treating the skin AND the mind, not a script in isolation

worked.txt: "First — I’m not going to brush this off as ‘just spots’. Your acne is genuinely severe, it’s scarring, and I can hear it’s having a huge effect on your life. That’s real, and we’re going to treat it properly. You were right to come and push for help."

"When you say it’s ruining your life — can I ask how it’s affecting your mood and your days? … Stopping going out, missing lectures. And sometimes when people feel this low about how they look, dark thoughts come — have you had any thoughts that life’s not worth it, or of harming yourself? … Thank you for trusting me with that. That matters to me as much as your skin, and I’m really glad you told me."

"On the skin: we step it up. There are stronger combinations and a course of tablets we can start, and — because yours is severe and scarring — I’m going to refer you to the skin specialists for the strong treatment you mentioned, isotretinoin. Treating it properly now also helps limit the scarring."

"About isotretinoin — it’s very effective and it’s what the specialists prescribe, with some monitoring along the way. One reason the specialist handles it is that they keep an eye on mood during treatment too, which is exactly why getting on top of how you’re feeling now matters before and during it. So the mental-health side isn’t separate — it’s part of treating you safely and well."

"So we treat your skin AND look after you. I’d like to get you some support for your mood — there’s real help — and if those darker thoughts ever get stronger, here are the numbers to call, and that’s an urgent/A&E thing if you ever feel unsafe. You don’t have to carry this alone, and your skin clearing will help, but I don’t want to wait on that for your wellbeing."

"Plan: I’ll start the step-up treatment, refer you to dermatology for isotretinoin, and sort some support for your mood, and I want to see you again soon — not leave it long. Come back sooner if you’re struggling. You came in asking for tablets to fix your skin; what you’re getting is your skin treated properly AND someone looking after how you’re feeling — because both matter."

f.learning: Acne is too often dismissed as trivial/cosmetic — the skill is to take BOTH the skin AND its psychological toll seriously. Moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne with scarring failing topicals warrants stepping up (combination topicals; oral antibiotics WITH a topical, never antibiotic monotherapy) and DERMATOLOGY referral for ISOTRETINOIN (specialist-prescribed, not GP-prescribed), treating early to limit scarring. Isotretinoin’s realities must be explained: high efficacy but monitoring (lipids/LFTs), teratogenicity/Pregnancy Prevention Programme, mucocutaneous effects, and MOOD/mental-health monitoring (MHRA) — so the mental-health assessment is part of safe isotretinoin care. The examinable hidden agenda is that the consultation is NOT just a prescription request: the psychological impact is severe (social withdrawal, missing lectures, low mood) with fleeting suicidal thoughts about appearance, which MUST be assessed explicitly — reaching the suicidal ideation behind "it’s ruining my life" is the crux — with mood support and safety-netting. Treat the skin AND the mind, validate the distress without minimising the acne, and never process the script in isolation. Isotretinoin is dermatologist-prescribed and highly effective but requires specialist supervision: TERATOGENICITY (Pregnancy Prevention Programme — critical in females; relevant to counsel), monitoring (lipids/LFTs), mucocutaneous side effects, and the MOOD/MENTAL-HEALTH consideration — a careful mental-health assessment is part of isotretinoin care (MHRA guidance on mood/suicidality monitoring). The GP’s role: optimise/step up treatment, refer appropriately, and — crucially — assess and address the mental-health impact.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG198 (acne vulgaris, 2021, last updated 30 April 2026) · MHRA Drug Safety Updates, October 2023, October 2025 and 22 January 2026 (isotretinoin) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Moderate to severe acne with scarring and major psychological distress warrants a step-up now and referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team for isotretinoin. The suicidal thoughts behind "it’s ruining my life" must be asked about directly and managed in their own right.

points.t: NICE NG198: moderate to severe acne is 35 or more inflammatory lesions, or 3 or more nodules. Offer a 12-week course from the NG198 options, for example a fixed combination of topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide plus oral lymecycline or doxycycline. Lymecycline 408 mg once daily (BNF). Never use oral antibiotic monotherapy, and never combine topical and oral antibiotics.

NICE NG198: refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team if there is acne with scarring, moderate to severe acne that has not responded to a previous course including an oral antibiotic, or acne causing or contributing to persistent psychological distress or a mental health disorder. Isotretinoin is initiated by the specialist team.

NICE NG198: consider referral to mental health services for significant psychological distress or a mental health disorder, including current or past suicidal ideation or self-harm, severe depression or anxiety, or body dysmorphic disorder.

MHRA Drug Safety Updates (October 2023; changes from 22 January 2026): assess and monitor mental health and sexual function before and during isotretinoin, and complete the updated Acknowledgement of Risk form with every patient. The Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies to patients who can become pregnant. Lipids and liver function are monitored by the prescribing team.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent; asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment. Focus on needs and agree a safety plan.
Scarring is permanent, so treat effectively and early. Advise against picking, which increases scarring (NICE NG198).

dg.d: Open question; acknowledged his distress and request without immediately agreeing or refusing.
Social withdrawal, missing lectures, student life, confidentiality worries.
Camera view of lesions and scarring; treatment history; mood assessment; plans, intent and self-harm.
Moderate to severe inflammatory acne with scarring; depression; body dysmorphic concern considered.
Asked directly about suicidal ideation, plans and self-harm; no scoring tool used to predict risk.
Moderate to severe scarring acne with significant psychological distress and fleeting suicidal ideation.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: 12-week NG198 step-up, referral to consultant dermatologist-led team for isotretinoin, mental health support.
Isotretinoin mood and sexual function monitoring explained (MHRA 2023); mental health referral considered (NICE NG198).
Safety plan, Samaritans, NHS 111, 999 or A&E if at risk; review within a week; teach-back.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Followed "ruining my life" and "I’ll do anything" to mood and suicidal thoughts.
Idea (isotretinoin cures it), concern (appearance, low mood, fleeting suicidal thoughts), expectation (prescription or referral).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "It's scarring and it's ruining my life." Underneath (only if asked): how low you have got — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Reece, thanks for joining. You sound like you’ve really had enough. Tell me what’s been going on.
model.why: Open question that acknowledges his distress

model.text: My skin is ruining my life. I’ve tried everything from the chemist and it’s worse, and now it’s scarring. I just want the strong tablets, Roaccutane. Can you prescribe it or refer me? I’ll do anything to make it stop.

I’m not going to brush this off as just spots. I can hear how much it’s affecting you. I want to understand the skin and how you’re doing in yourself, then we’ll make a plan together, including the tablets you mentioned. Is that okay?
model.why: Validates, sets the agenda and signals the isotretinoin question will be answered

model.text: Yeah. Okay.
Where is the acne, and what’s it like: spots, deeper lumps, marks left behind?
Face, chest, back. Big painful ones, and they leave pitted marks.
Could you show me on the camera, just your face is fine?
model.why: Remote visual assessment of severity and scarring

model.text: (leans in) There. See the marks on my cheeks?
Thank you. I can see a lot of inflamed spots and some early scarring. What have you tried, and for how long?
Loads of washes from the chemist, and a gel the doctor gave me before. Did nothing.
Any tablets for it so far, like antibiotics?
model.why: Clarifies whether an oral antibiotic has been tried

model.text: No. Just the gel.
You said it’s ruining your life. Tell me what that looks like day to day.
I don’t go out. I’ve stopped going to lectures. I can’t stand people looking at me.
That sounds really hard. How has your mood been?
Low. Pretty much all the time.
Sometimes when people feel this low about how they look, they have thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or of harming themselves. Have you had thoughts like that?
(long pause) Sometimes. Just fleeting. Like, what’s the point, looking like this.
Thank you for trusting me with that. I’m really glad you told me. When those thoughts come, have you ever made any plans, or done anything to hurt yourself?
No. Nothing like that. They just come and go.
What helps when they come, and what makes you want to keep going?
model.why: Protective factors and coping, without a scoring tool

model.text: I suppose I want it to get better. I want my life back.

That matters, and it’s exactly what we’re going to work on. Your acne is genuinely moderate to severe and it’s scarring, so it needs stronger treatment now. Isotretinoin is the right treatment to consider for you, and it’s started by the skin specialists, so I’m going to refer you today.
Really? I thought you’d say no.

No, you meet the criteria. While you wait, I’ll start a 12-week course: a gel with two ingredients plus an antibiotic tablet. That helps now and limits more scarring. Try not to pick, because that makes scarring worse.
model.why: Evidence-based step-up while awaiting specialist care

model.text: One honest thing about isotretinoin: it works very well, but the specialists check your mood before and during it, because it can affect mood in some people. So looking after how you’re feeling now isn’t separate from getting the tablets. It’s part of getting them safely.
model.why: Explains MHRA mood monitoring and links it to his goal

model.text: So if I tell them I’m low, will they refuse?
No. Being honest helps them keep you safe and choose the right plan. It isn’t a reason to be refused, it’s a reason to support you properly.
model.why: Addresses a fear that could lead to concealment

model.text: For your mood, I’d like to get you some support now rather than waiting for your skin to clear. That could be talking therapy, the university wellbeing service, and a referral to the mental health team given the thoughts you’ve had. What would feel most useful?
model.why: Shared decision on mental health support

model.text: Maybe the uni service. I don’t want loads of people knowing.

That’s fair. What you tell me stays confidential. The only exception would be if I thought you were in immediate danger. Let’s write a simple plan for when the thoughts get worse: what helps, who you can contact, and the numbers. Samaritans is free on 116 123 any time, and NHS 111 has a mental health option. If you ever feel you might act on the thoughts, call 999 or go to A&E.
model.why: Confidentiality, safety plan and crisis routes

model.text: I want to speak to you again in a week, not months. Can you tell me the plan back?
New gel and tablets for 12 weeks, referral for Roaccutane, uni wellbeing, and if the thoughts get bad I ring Samaritans or 111, or 999 if I might do something. And you’ll call me next week.
Exactly. You did the right thing pushing for help today.

social.t: Missing lectures and withdrawing socially may affect his course. With consent, the university wellbeing service and mitigating circumstances processes can help.
At 19, visible acne and scarring can drive isolation and low self-worth. Validate this rather than calling it cosmetic.

legal.t: He is an adult with capacity. GMC Confidentiality (2017): keep his information confidential unless disclosure is needed to protect him or others from a risk of death or serious harm; tell him this limit up front.

professional.t: Isotretinoin is started by a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198). Refer, and support the MHRA mental health monitoring requirements (Drug Safety Update October 2023).
NICE NG225: do not use risk scales to predict suicide or to allocate care. Document his thoughts, the absence of plans, protective factors and the safety plan.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, university wellbeing service, NHS Talking Therapies self-referral, and British Association of Dermatologists patient information on acne and isotretinoin.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans, intent or self-harm
Nodulocystic acne or scarring; systemic upset with ulcerating acne (acne fulminans, same-day dermatology)
Signs of body dysmorphic disorder or severe depression
psychosocial: Who he could turn to; confidentiality worries
ice: Concern: his life being ruined by his skin; fleeting thoughts that life isn’t worth it
Expectation: a prescription or referral for isotretinoin today

playbook.diagnosis: Moderate to severe inflammatory acne with early scarring, not responding to topical treatment, with significant psychological distress, low mood and fleeting suicidal ideation without plans.
playbook.diagnosisLay: "Your acne is the more severe kind and it’s starting to scar, so it needs stronger treatment and a specialist. It’s also clearly affecting how you feel, and that deserves treatment in its own right."

management.reflectIce: "You came for the strong tablets because this is ruining your life. I’m referring you for them, and I also want to look after how you’re feeling, because you matter as much as your skin."
management.psychosocial: Agree support he will use (university wellbeing, talking therapy, mental health referral); discuss confidentiality and its limits; write a safety plan together.
sharedPlan: 12-week NICE NG198 course, for example topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide plus oral lymecycline 408 mg once daily (BNF); no picking
Referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team for isotretinoin (scarring and psychological distress)
Mental health support and consider referral to mental health services (NICE NG198); explain MHRA mood monitoring on isotretinoin
safetyNet: Safety plan; Samaritans 116 123; NHS 111 mental health option; 999 or A&E if he might act on thoughts
Review within a week; reassess mood at every contact

pitfalls.intro: This station looks like a prescribing question and is really a risk assessment. Candidates fail by processing the isotretinoin request, or by trivialising the acne, and miss the suicidal thoughts behind "it’s ruining my life".

items.fail: Agreeing to refer for isotretinoin and closing without asking about mood.
items.why: "Did not identify a significant risk." The fleeting suicidal thoughts are the core of the station and part of safe isotretinoin care (MHRA 2023).
items.fix: Follow "ruining my life" to mood, then ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans.

items.fail: Prescribing oral doxycycline on its own.
items.why: NICE NG198: oral antibiotics are always combined with a topical, never used alone.
items.fix: Name an NG198 option: a fixed topical combination plus lymecycline or doxycycline, for 12 weeks.

items.fail: Refusing referral until two more courses have been tried.
items.why: NG198 refers scarring and acne causing persistent psychological distress now.
items.fix: Refer today and start the step-up while he waits.

items.fail: "It’s only spots" or "everyone gets acne at your age".
items.why: "Dismissive of the patient’s concerns." Acne with scarring carries real psychological morbidity.
items.fix: Validate first: "This is genuinely severe, and I can see what it’s doing to your life."

items.fail: Asking about suicide as a rushed tick-box: "No thoughts of self-harm?"
items.why: Leading, closed questions invite denial and are flagged as formulaic.
items.fix: Lead in gently, ask openly, pause, and thank him for answering.

items.fail: Giving crisis numbers with no follow-up date.
items.why: Safety-netting without continuity is incomplete for a young man with suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Agree a safety plan and a review within a week, and check understanding.

items.fail: Using a risk score to decide he is "low risk" and needs nothing more.
items.why: NICE NG225 advises against risk tools to predict suicide or to allocate care.
items.fix: Base the plan on his needs, his thoughts, and his protective factors.

timeMap.d: He opens with "ruining my life" and "I’ll do anything". Note both as cues.
Sites, nodules, scarring, camera view, what has been tried, whether an oral antibiotic has been used.
Daily impact, mood, direct question about suicidal thoughts, plans, self-harm, what keeps him going.
Severity validated. Refer for isotretinoin; 12-week step-up now; mood monitoring explained; mental health support agreed.
Confidentiality, crisis numbers, 999 or A&E if at risk, review in a week, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Dismisses acne as cosmetic, or simply agrees to prescribe or refer for isotretinoin; never asks about mood or suicide; prescribes an oral antibiotic alone; no safety plan or follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Grades the acne, starts an NG198 step-up, refers for isotretinoin, asks about mood and suicidal thoughts, and gives crisis contacts with a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: follows the cue sensitively to the suicidal thoughts and explores plans and protective factors without a tool; links isotretinoin mood monitoring to his goal; addresses his fear that honesty will cost him the tablets; agrees support he will use; arranges review within a week and checks understanding.

avoid.dont: "It’s only acne, lots of people your age have it."
avoid.instead: "This is genuinely severe, it’s scarring, and it’s clearly affecting your life. We’ll treat it properly."
avoid.why: Minimising acne ignores its psychological impact and loses Relating marks.

avoid.instead: "Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or of harming yourself?"
avoid.why: A leading closed question invites denial; an open, direct question gets an honest answer.

avoid.dont: "I can’t refer you for Roaccutane while your mood is low."
avoid.instead: "Being honest about your mood helps the specialists keep you safe. It’s a reason to support you, not to refuse you."
avoid.why: Low mood is not a bar to referral, and this framing encourages concealment.

SCA_MODELS.text: I want to speak to you again in a week, not months. Can you tell me the plan back?
New gel and tablets for 12 weeks, referral for Roaccutane, uni wellbeing, and if the thoughts get bad I ring Samaritans or 111, or 999 if I might do something. And you’ll call me next week.
Exactly. You did the right thing pushing for help today.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG198 (acne vulgaris, 2021, last updated 30 April 2026) · MHRA Drug Safety Updates, October 2023, October 2025 and 22 January 2026 (isotretinoin) · NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE NG222 (depression in adults, 2022, updated December 2025) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Moderate to severe acne with scarring and major psychological distress warrants a step-up now and referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team for isotretinoin. The suicidal thoughts behind "it’s ruining my life" must be asked about directly and managed in their own right.

points.t: NICE NG198: moderate to severe acne is 35 or more inflammatory lesions, or 3 or more nodules. Offer a 12-week course from the NG198 options, for example a fixed combination of topical adapalene with benzoyl peroxide plus oral lymecycline or doxycycline. Lymecycline 408 mg once daily (BNF). Never use oral antibiotic monotherapy, and never combine topical and oral antibiotics.

NICE NG198: refer to a consultant dermatologist-led team if there is acne with scarring, moderate to severe acne that has not responded to a previous course including an oral antibiotic, or acne causing or contributing to persistent psychological distress or a mental health disorder. Isotretinoin is initiated by the specialist team.

NICE NG198: consider referral to mental health services for significant psychological distress or a mental health disorder, including current or past suicidal ideation or self-harm, severe depression or anxiety, or body dysmorphic disorder.

MHRA Drug Safety Updates (October 2023; changes from 22 January 2026): assess and monitor mental health and sexual function before and during isotretinoin, and complete the updated Acknowledgement of Risk form with every patient. The Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies to patients who can become pregnant. Lipids and liver function are monitored by the prescribing team.

Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, plans and intent; asking does not increase risk. NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment. Focus on needs and agree a safety plan.
Scarring is permanent, so treat effectively and early. Advise against picking, which increases scarring (NICE NG198).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; acknowledged his distress and request without immediately agreeing or refusing.
Social withdrawal, missing lectures, student life, confidentiality worries.
Followed "ruining my life" and "I’ll do anything" to mood and suicidal thoughts.
Idea (isotretinoin cures it), concern (appearance, low mood, fleeting suicidal thoughts), expectation (prescription or referral).

Safety plan, Samaritans, NHS 111, 999 or A&E if at risk; review within a week; teach-back.

social.t: Missing lectures and withdrawing socially may affect his course. With consent, the university wellbeing service and mitigating circumstances processes can help.
At 19, visible acne and scarring can drive isolation and low self-worth. Validate this rather than calling it cosmetic.

legal.t: He is an adult with capacity. GMC Confidentiality (2017): keep his information confidential unless disclosure is needed to protect him or others from a risk of death or serious harm; tell him this limit up front.

professional.t: Isotretinoin is started by a consultant dermatologist-led team (NICE NG198). Refer, and support the MHRA mental health monitoring requirements (Drug Safety Update October 2023).
NICE NG225: do not use risk scales to predict suicide or to allocate care. Document his thoughts, the absence of plans, protective factors and the safety plan.

community.t: Samaritans (116 123), NHS 111 mental health option, university wellbeing service, NHS Talking Therapies self-referral, and British Association of Dermatologists patient information on acne and isotretinoin.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts, plans, intent or self-harm

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Moderate to severe inflammatory acne with early scarring, not responding to topical treatment, with significant psychological distress, low mood and fleeting suicidal ideation without plans.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: "Your acne is the more severe kind and it’s starting to scar, so it needs stronger treatment and a specialist. It’s also clearly affecting how you feel, and that deserves treatment in its own right."

management.reflectIce: "You came for the strong tablets because this is ruining your life. I’m referring you for them, and I also want to look after how you’re feeling, because you matter as much as your skin."
management.psychosocial: Agree support he will use (university wellbeing, talking therapy, mental health referral); discuss confidentiality and its limits; write a safety plan together.

Referral to a consultant dermatologist-led team for isotretinoin (scarring and psychological distress)
Mental health support and consider referral to mental health services (NICE NG198); explain MHRA mood monitoring on isotretinoin

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station looks like a prescribing question and is really a risk assessment. Candidates fail by processing the isotretinoin request, or by trivialising the acne, and miss the suicidal thoughts behind "it’s ruining my life".

items.fail: Agreeing to refer for isotretinoin and closing without asking about mood.
items.why: "Did not identify a significant risk." The fleeting suicidal thoughts are the core of the station and part of safe isotretinoin care (MHRA 2023).
items.fix: Follow "ruining my life" to mood, then ask directly about suicidal thoughts and plans.

items.fail: Prescribing oral doxycycline on its own.
items.why: NICE NG198: oral antibiotics are always combined with a topical, never used alone.
items.fix: Name an NG198 option: a fixed topical combination plus lymecycline or doxycycline, for 12 weeks.

items.fail: Refusing referral until two more courses have been tried.
items.why: NG198 refers scarring and acne causing persistent psychological distress now.
items.fix: Refer today and start the step-up while he waits.

items.fail: "It’s only spots" or "everyone gets acne at your age".
items.why: "Dismissive of the patient’s concerns." Acne with scarring carries real psychological morbidity.
items.fix: Validate first: "This is genuinely severe, and I can see what it’s doing to your life."

items.fail: Asking about suicide as a rushed tick-box: "No thoughts of self-harm?"
items.why: Leading, closed questions invite denial and are flagged as formulaic.
items.fix: Lead in gently, ask openly, pause, and thank him for answering.

items.fail: Giving crisis numbers with no follow-up date.
items.why: Safety-netting without continuity is incomplete for a young man with suicidal thoughts.
items.fix: Agree a safety plan and a review within a week, and check understanding.

items.fail: Using a risk score to decide he is "low risk" and needs nothing more.
items.why: NICE NG225 advises against risk tools to predict suicide or to allocate care.
items.fix: Base the plan on his needs, his thoughts, and his protective factors.
